dynamical-behavior-of-engineering-struct.caption: Figure 4a. Wavenumber against frequency for the same SAFE branches shown in Figure 4, with a logarithmic wavenumber axis in radians per metre. Select bar, I-beam, rail, pipe or plate, and drag the wave markers to compare their wavenumbers. The plate is 10 mm thick and infinite across its width, with A0 and S0 Lamb waves and SH0 shear-horizontal waves. Wavenumber is computed as k = 2πf/cₚ = 2π/λ. The educational rail-like section is 35 × 40 mm; its mode count differs from a full-size railway rail. The refined meshes are checked against finer meshes. Wave packets travel at group velocity while their crests travel at phase velocity.

machine-learning-the-complete-picture-an.caption: Figure 3a. Three forecasting methods fitted to the same synthetic monthly sensor signal: (a) seasonal ARIMA, (b) additive Holt-Winters exponential smoothing and (c) gradient boosted trees with lagged inputs. Each method forecasts 24 months using only the history before the selected origin. Withheld observations appear after the forecasts, with RMSE and MAE measured over all 24 months. Tree forecasts recursively use their own predictions as future lag inputs. The shaded interval in (a) is the ARIMA model's 95% prediction interval. Choose month 120, 156 or 192 to compare different histories; the relative performance changes with the origin.

Figure 6a. Three feature-selection methods on one reproducible synthetic regression example, with 360 training rows and 120 held-out test rows. The target depends on x1 (energy), x2 (duration) and x3 (frequency); x4 is a noisy copy of x1, and x5 and x6 are nuisance inputs. (a) A Filter ranks absolute Pearson correlations and keeps three features. (b) A Wrapper adds features using five-fold cross-validation, fitting its scaler inside each fold. Move the step slider to inspect candidate subsets. (c) An Embedded method uses Lasso: increasing the L1 penalty shrinks coefficients toward zero. The dashed line marks α = 0.12. The same Ridge predictor evaluates each selected feature set on the held-out rows, which never influence selection or scaling.

add.caption: Figure 2. Signal processing and system identification on one problem. A swept sine x(t), from 0.3 to 1.7 Hz over 12 s, drives a damped resonator with impulse response h(t) (fₙ = 1 Hz, ζ = 0.1), and its output y(t) is measured with noise 20 dB below it. The least squares estimate fits a model's output to the measured one: gradient descent on the squared error walks across its contours from a first guess (0.85 Hz, 0.27) to the estimate fₙ = 0.9995 Hz, ζ = 0.1004, while the model's impulse response and output settle onto the system's.

Figure 7. Six types of optimization problem and the methods that solve them, each a small problem solved exactly; choose one with the buttons, or let the figure step through all six. Beside the plot, the four characteristics (i) to (iv) are marked for the problem shown, with the methods that solve it (the one drawn has a key). Convex: gradient descent reaches the single minimum of a convex quadratic from all three starts. Linear program: the simplex method walks from vertex to vertex to the optimum (3.5, 0.5), where 3x₁ + 2x₂ = 11.5, and the interior point method's central path crosses the feasible region to the same vertex. Nonconvex: on a function with four minima, gradient descent stops in a local minimum (f = −50.06), while a swarm of 16 particles first gathers in another basin and then finds the global one (f = −78.33). Constrained: a quadratic penalty with μ from 0.1 to 100 moves the minimum of the penalized function to within 0.007 of the constrained optimum on the boundary. Multi-objective: NSGA-II evolves 40 candidates onto the exact Pareto front f₂ = 1 − √f₁.

add.caption: Figure 9. Four global optimization algorithms on one landscape with seven minima: (a) a genetic algorithm, (b) particle swarm optimization, (c) simulated annealing and (d) continuous ant colony optimization (ACO<sub>R</sub>), each allowed the same 400 evaluations of the objective, a shallow bowl with seven Gaussian wells whose global minimum, f* = −1.788, lies at (2.13, −1.74). GA, PSO and ACO<sub>R</sub> start from the same 20 random points, the best of which lies in the second deepest well (upper left); SA starts from the first of them. In (a) thin lines join each child to the two tournament winners it was bred from, and a dotted segment is a mutation; in (b) each particle flies along its velocity arrow, pulled toward its own best point (pale line) and the swarm's best; in (c) the walker accepts uphill steps (open rings) less and less often as the temperature T falls from 2 to 0.002, and its rejected proposals fade in gray; in (d) the ellipses are the Gaussian kernels of a ranked archive of the 20 best points, the pheromone from which new ants are drawn. Crimson marks each method's best point so far. (e) The best value found against the evaluations used: the four reach the global well after 29, 69, 82 and 73 evaluations and end 3.9 × 10⁻⁵, 8.8 × 10⁻⁴, 7.2 × 10⁻³ and 3.7 × 10⁻⁹ above f*. Over 200 seeds they end in its basin in 95%, 89.5%, 96.5% and 98.5% of runs, against 31.8% for a gradient-based local search from a random start.

add.caption: Figure 4. Undoing a blur, an ill-posed inverse problem. (a) A hidden cause m, a smooth bump and a sharp block on 64 cells, is blurred by a Gaussian kernel G and measured with noise, d = Gm + e. (b) The cause recovered from d: without regularization the estimate reaches 1.7 × 10¹³ and changes completely with each noise draw (Hadamard's third condition failing), while Tikhonov regularization at the discrepancy principle, α = 0.087, recovers m with a 17.6% error, close to the lowest possible 17.4% (α = 0.062). (c) The L-curve, solution norm against residual norm, one point per regularization strength: the discrepancy principle takes the point where the residual equals the noise level, and the corner, at α = 0.014, gives 23.1%. (d) The Picard plot: the singular values sᵢ fall from 0.99 to below 10⁻¹⁶ while the data coefficients |uᵢᵀd| level off at the noise floor near i = 17, and the filter factors fᵢ, in the strip below, switch off the terms beyond it. Choose the method, the strength (or sweep it), the noise level and the noise draw; the numbers are for 1% noise, draw 1.

Figure 5. Solving by iterating, where the iteration count is the regularization parameter. The blurred data of Figure 4 (1% noise) solved from m = 0 by Landweber iteration (gradient descent, ω = 1/s₁²) and by conjugate gradients (CGLS). (a) The current iterate against the true cause. (b) The iterate as a filter on the Picard plot of Figure 4: its filter factors fᵢ open towards the small singular values as k grows. (c) The error against the truth falls, then rises again (semi-convergence): CGLS reaches its lowest error, 17.2%, at k = 14, and Landweber the same 17.2% at k = 177, both as low as the best Tikhonov solution (17.4%). (d) The residual only ever falls; stopping where it reaches the noise level σ√N (the discrepancy principle) gives k = 7 for CGLS and k = 32 for Landweber, with errors of 18.1% and 18.4%.

Figure 6. Finite element model updating, a nonlinear inverse problem. (a) The misfit Φ between the measured and the computed natural frequencies of a two-storey shear building (floors of 100 t; measured 3.193 Hz and 7.766 Hz, 0.3% high and 0.4% low against the true building, k₁ = 120 and k₂ = 80 MN/m) holds two exact fits in one long curved valley, (124.8, 76.7) MN/m next to the true building and its twin (153.5, 62.4) MN/m, because the frequencies fix only k₁ + 2k₂ and k₁k₂, which swapping (k₁, k₂) for (2k₂, k₁/2) keeps; the dashed line k₁ = 2k₂ is the mirror between them. From (210, 30), Gauss-Newton (6 iterations, 7 forward-model runs), Levenberg-Marquardt (7 iterations, 15 runs) and gradient descent (249 iterations, 750 runs) all converge on the twin; the particle swarm (1,988 runs) lands on the twin here and on the true side for 51.6% of 500 random seeds, and MCMC puts 49% of its 16,000 samples on the true side of the dashed line, where the exact posterior has exactly half. (b) The misfit against the number of forward-model runs, or, for MCMC, the histogram of k₁ over the exact posterior. Adding the measured first-mode shape (amplitude ratio 2.04, against 2.10 for the true-side fit and 2.81 for the twin) removes the twin altogether, while a prior at the design values (100 MN/m ± 35%) leaves it a local minimum that still traps the local solvers and keeps 26% of the posterior.

add.caption: Figure 12. One signal at two sensors, recovered by generalized cross-correlation and a Wiener filter. The signal, eight impact responses of an 11 Hz mode, reaches sensor 2 48 ms after sensor 1, and each sensor adds its own white noise, here at −10 dB; the figure steps through the method by itself, and a click on a stage jumps to it. (a) The two records: the clean signal, the noisy records with the clean signal drawn on top (the method never sees it), sensor 2 advanced by the estimated delay, their average, and the Wiener-filtered estimate ŝ(t) and its delayed copy (crimson) against the true signals (dashed). (b) The cross-correlation of the two records with each frequency weighted by γ²/(1 − γ²), where γ² is their coherence; its peak, read to the nearest sample, gives τ̂ = 50 ms against the true 48 ms. (c) After alignment, the spectrum of the average, the cross-spectrum the two records have in common, and the Wiener gain G they give, with the coherence γ² (dashed). The estimate correlates with the true signal at ρ = 0.855, an SNR of 4.4 dB, 14.5 dB above the record; the signal and the SNR (−30 to 20 dB) can be chosen at the bottom right.

Figure 13. One signal at two sensors, recovered after averaging repeated shots. The same signal and delay as in Figure 12, now at −20 dB per shot: the excitation is fired M times with new noise in each shot, and the averaged records go through the steps of Figure 12, with the delay refined below one sample. (a) One shot's records, their average over M = 64 shots, measured 18.1 dB cleaner as 10 log₁₀ 64 predicts, and the estimate (crimson) against the true signals (dashed); (b) the cross-correlation, whose peak, refined by a parabola through it and its neighbours, gives τ̂ = 48.2 ms; (c) the spectra and the Wiener gain after alignment. The table compares 1 to 1,024 shots at the chosen SNR: one shot finds a noise peak at −101.9 ms (ρ = 0.00), while from 16 shots on the delay stays within one sample of 48 ms and the correlation rises from 0.90 to 1.00 (0.967 at 64 shots).

Figure 10. Blind source separation, method 1: kurtosis ICA. Two sensors record x = As + n, mixtures of a harmonic excitation and a train of impact responses plus white Gaussian noise; the figure steps through the sources, the mixing, the whitening z = Wx (cov z = I) and the rotation y = R(θ)z that maximizes K(θ) = |kurt y₁| + |kurt y₂|, shown as (a) the two channels over the 4 s record, (b) their joint scatter with the images of the two source axes and (c) K(θ), drawn on one scale for every SNR. At the default 10 dB the maximum is at θ = −30.5°, and the estimates, matched to their sources in order and sign, correlate with them at 0.841 and 0.830 (SIR 6.7 and 15.3 dB). Click a step to jump to it, or choose the sensor SNR from −30 to 40 dB: the curve flattens with the noise and the separation fails near 0 dB. Each stage is drawn in units of its RMS, and the record is the 4 s record of Figure 11.

Figure 11. Blind source separation, method 2: SOBI-family separation and Wiener denoising. On the same records as Figure 10, the sensors' spectra (c) show the white noise as a flat floor, estimated as their median, and the bands where the sources rise above it; whitening uses only those bands' cross-spectral matrices with the floor removed, a single rotation then diagonalizes all of them at once ((d), the off-diagonal energy left against the angle), and a Wiener filter keeps each output's bands above its own noise (the gains under (c)), while (a) and (b) show the signals and their joint scatter at each step. At the default 0 dB and 4 s the method separates the sources with SIRs of 32.4 and 19.0 dB, against −0.4 and 3.2 dB for kurtosis ICA on the same data, and the Wiener filter raises the correlations from 0.471 and 0.520 to 0.940 and 0.923. Choose a step, the sensor SNR (−30 to 40 dB) or the record length (4, 16 or 64 s): both SIRs stay above 10 dB down to −15 dB at 4 s, and a longer record sharpens the separation.
